by taking complements ([[thm-continuity-from-above-for-measures]]).

## Statement

Assume AC. For $d\ge1$, let $\gamma_d$ be standard Gaussian measure on $\mathbb R^d$,
let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be Borel, and let
$A+rB_2^d=\{a+ru:a\in A,\ |u|\le1\}$. Then for every $r\ge0$,
$$\gamma_{d,*}(A+rB_2^d)\ge \Phi\!\left(\Phi^{-1}(\gamma_d(A))+r\right),$$
where $\gamma_{d,*}(S)=\sup\{\gamma_d(K):K\subseteq S,\ K\text{ compact}\}$ is Gaussian inner measure, and $\Phi^{-1}(0)=-\infty$, $\Phi^{-1}(1)=+\infty$.


## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $d\ge1$, standard Gaussian measure $\gamma_d$, a Borel set $A$, and $r\ge0$.

[F1] The scalar standard normal has density $\varphi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$, and $\Phi$ is continuous and strictly increasing with limits $0$ and $1$ at the two infinities. Independent standard Gaussian vectors form a joint Gaussian vector, and orthogonal linear combinations have their stated Gaussian laws. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], [[def-multivariate-normal-law]], [[lem-finite-independent-gaussian-vectors-form-joint-multivariate-normal]], [[lem-standard-normal-cdf-is-continuous-and-strictly-increasing]].

[F2] Differentiation under the integral follows from an integrable majorant, dominated convergence passes dominated limits, and Fubini applies to absolutely integrable functions. [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]], [[thm-dominated-convergence]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]].

[F3] Integration by parts and the fundamental theorem apply on one-dimensional absolutely continuous slices. AC implies their DC and Countable Choice assumptions. [[thm-integration-by-parts-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]], [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F4] Borel probabilities on Polish spaces are inner regular. [[thm-borel-probability-measures-on-polish-spaces-are-inner-regular]].

[F5] A unit-mass smooth bump gives the scaled convolution family. One may choose it nonnegative and supported in the unit ball by normalizing $\exp(-1/(1-|x|^2))\mathbf1_{\{|x|<1\}}$. [[def-mollifier-family-generated-by-a-unit-mass-smooth-bump]].

[F6] Under Countable Choice, the nonnegative Lebesgue change-of-variables theorem applies to Euclidean dilations and orthogonal maps; hence a ball of radius $R$ has volume $v_dR^d$ with finite $v_d$ bounded by the volume of the containing cube. [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]].

[F7] The exponential derivative, the derivative-of-inverse rule at a nonzero derivative, and the chain rule apply to the scalar functions below. [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]], [[thm-chain-rule]].

[F8] A continuous real-valued function on a closed interval takes every value between its endpoint values. [[thm-intermediate-value]].

For $h\ne0$, the density formula gives $[\Phi(x+h)-\Phi(x)]/h=h^{-1}\int_x^{x+h}\varphi(s)\,ds$, which tends to $\varphi(x)$ by continuity; hence $\Phi'(x)=\varphi(x)>0$. The CDF lemma gives continuity, strict increase and limits $0,1$ at the two infinities. For any $u\in(0,1)$, choose $a<b$ with $\Phi(a)<u<\Phi(b)$ using those limits; [F8] applied to $\Phi$ on $[a,b]$ gives an $x$ with $\Phi(x)=u$, and strict increase makes it unique. Thus $\Phi$ is a bijection onto $(0,1)$. Set $I(u)=\varphi(\Phi^{-1}(u))$ for $0<u<1$, and set $I(0)=I(1)=0$. $$\gamma_{d,*}(A+rB_2^d)\ge \Phi\!\left(\Phi^{-1}(\gamma_d(A))+r\right),$$

$$\int_a^bFG'+\int_a^bF'G=F(b)G(b)-F(a)G(a).$$

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume countable choice. If $P$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure on $P$, then for every Borel $A\subseteq P$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ and $b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}$ be
reals, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then

$$\Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big)^{2} \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}\Big),$$

and, in root form ([[thm-of-square-roots]]),

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big| \;\le\; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}} \; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}}.$$

Equality holds in the first display if and only if the two lists are
proportional, in the symmetric sense that there is a pair
$(\lambda, \mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda a_k = \mu b_k$ for every
$k < n$.

**No root is used in the proof of the squared form.** That form is an identity
plus a sign argument in the ordered field, and the root form is only a
restatement of it through the monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives
([[lem-of-square-monotone]]); the root enters nowhere but the last step, where
that restatement is made and [[thm-of-square-roots]] is what supplies the
square-root symbol. This matters here, because it makes the squared
inequality independent of the existence theorem for roots.

Let $a\le b$ and $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]). The function $f$ is
**absolutely continuous** on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$\delta>0$ such that every finite family of subintervals
$[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, indexed by $j<m$, whose open interiors are pairwise
disjoint and which satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}(v_j-u_j)<\delta$$

also satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}|f(v_j)-f(u_j)|<\varepsilon.$$

Finite sums and the empty sum are those of [[def-finite-sum]] and
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. For $m=0$ both sums are $0$, so the condition is
automatic. On $[a,a]$ every permitted interval is a singleton and every endpoint
increment is $0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), so every function on that singleton is
absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity implies ordinary continuity
([[def-continuity-real]]); that implication is proved next rather than built into
the definition.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.
